title: Kinetic Theory for the Shear Viscosity of Dense Binary Dipolar Fluid Mixtures
authors: Christopher Devik Fjeldstad, Roberto Troncoso, Astrid S. de Wijn
abstract: We construct a kinetic theory for the shear viscosity of dense binary fluid mixtures of strongly-interacting dipolar hard spheres. We derive an expression for the pairwise correlations in the binary mixtures that is accurate up to packing fractions around 0.35. The approach is based on Enskog-Thorne theory, and inspired by the theory for dense pure fluids developed by Pousaneh and de Wijn. It relies on effective coupling parameters obtained from the pure fluids combined with mixing rules and a heuristic expression for the collision integral. We compare our results to viscosities obtained numerically from molecular-dynamics simulations of dipolar hard-sphere fluids. Our expression for the shear viscosity of the binary mixtures captures the density and composition dependent behavior of the binary dipolar fluids up to packing fraction of $ξ\lesssim 0.3$ without any mixture-derived fit parameters.
summary: This paper develops an advanced kinetic theory for calculating the shear viscosity of binary mixtures of dipolar hard spheres. By extending Enskog-Thorne theory and incorporating structural corrections, the authors derive an accurate expression that matches molecular dynamics simulations across a range of densities. It provides a robust theoretical tool for understanding transport properties in complex, strongly interacting classical fluids.
main_problem: The primary goal is constructing a kinetic theory for the shear viscosity of dense binary fluid mixtures composed of strongly-interacting dipolar hard spheres.
main_result: The derived expression successfully captures the density and composition dependence of the shear viscosity up to packing fractions around 0.3 without requiring mixture-derived fit parameters, showing good agreement with molecular dynamics simulations.
method: The approach extends Enskog-Thorne theory, building upon Pousaneh and de Wijn's work for pure dipolar fluids by incorporating structural corrections derived from cluster expansions and resumming the residual dipolar contributions exponentially.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a binary mixture of Dipolar Hard Spheres (DHS). The interactions include both hard-core repulsion and long-range dipole-dipole forces, making it a complex many-body classical fluid system.
key_observables: Shear viscosity ($\eta$), partial pair distribution functions ($\chi_{ij}$), and effective collision cross sections ($\Omega_{	ext{bmDHS}, ij}$).
important_parameters: Packing fraction ($\xi$), dipolar coupling constants ($\lambda_{ii}$, $\lambda_{jj}$), and particle sizes ($\sigma_i$). The theory is tested in regimes where dipolar energy can be much larger than $k_B T$.
main_assumptions: The theory assumes momentum transfer is dominated by hard-sphere core collisions, allowing the use of Enskog-Thorne formalism. It relies on approximations like replacing the hard-sphere contribution with BMCSL results and resumming dipolar terms exponentially.
figures_summary: Figures compare the predicted shear viscosity ($\eta$) for mixtures with equally sized cores and those with differently sized cores across various combinations of dipolar coupling constants, showing good agreement with simulation data up to $\xi \approx 0.3$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the framework based on Enskog-Thorne theory for binary mixtures. It then details the necessary structural inputs ($\chi_{ij}$) by correcting cluster expansion results, leading to the final expression for shear viscosity, which is validated against molecular dynamics simulations.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluids, the rigorous application of kinetic theory and the handling of long-range, anisotropic interactions (dipoles) in a dense fluid context provide valuable methodological insights applicable to complex quantum many-body systems where simple approximations fail.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Prediction for χDHS i using the cluster expansion de- rived by Novak et al. [8] in the pure limit (full lines) along with, for comparison, the equivalent prediction using pDHS theory for pure fluids [7] (dashed lines). At low density, as long as λi ≲2, the Novak et al. prediction is very similar to pDHS theory. However, the higher-order terms in the density become significant, and Novak et al.’s expansion for mixtures fails.

FIG. 2. Prediction for χDHS i in the pure limit: fully corrected expression for χij, denoted bmDHS theory (full lines), the equivalent prediction using pDHS theory for pure fluids [7] (dashed lines), and only the BMCSL correct for the hard- sphere contribution (dotted lines). Although some improve- ment can be seen in the latter, especially for weak dipoles, it still fails when λi = 4. In contrast, bmDHS theory, which uses both corrections, shows far better agreement with pDHS theory, although very strong dipoles still present an quan- titative issue. Crucially, bmDHS theory satisfies the sanity requirement that χDHS i > 0 for all densities.

FIG. 3. Rescaled shear viscosity from simulations for pure DHS fluids with λ = 1, 2, 3 and 4. The rescaling uses the Enskog expression for a pure hard-sphere fluid at the same volume fraction with σ∗ i = 1, mass m∗ i = 1, and reduced tem- perature T ∗= 1.5. The predictions are made using bmDHS theory for fluids with small particles (σ∗ i = 1, m∗ i = 1) (a) and large particle fluids (σ∗ i = 1.5, m∗ i = 3.375) (b). The associated fit parameters can be found in tables I.
